b: Reading the literature on how to detect consciousness in animals can be discouraging. Consciousness cannot be measured directly. The indicators we have were developed in humans, and it is unclear whether they are valid for other species. Some have concluded that questions such as whether fishes feel pain could never be settled empirically, and that we should remain agnostic.

This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic. Together with Heather Browning, I give many reasons to be sceptical about current measures of nonhuman consciousness. We do not, however, see these problems as fatal.

When measuring some target state, we often use indicators or proxy measures. One crucial feature we require of the indicators we use is that they are valid, that is, that they are actually measuring the intended target. In most cases, all that is needed is to establish a correlation between the indicator and the target.
Consciousness, however, cannot be directly measured. Without knowing in advance which individuals are conscious and which are not, we are not equipped with any means of testing our indicators.

In cases such as these, we must instead use background assumptions that link the target to the indicator. The trouble is that almost all of the currently developed indicators use the same controversial background assumption, namely, that what separates conscious from unconscious processing in humans also separates conscious beings from nonconscious ones. The convergence of evidence from such sources gives us no further assurance that they are hitting the relevant target.

Instead, we advocate a more pluralistic method, using something like robustness analysis, where a result that remains invariant under different experiments, models, and background assumptions can be considered more robustly supported. With multiple lines of evidence, tested against one another, and using independent background assumptions, we can infer that the best explanation for observed differences is differences in consciousness.

While the presence of one type of evidence for consciousness may be considered insufficient, when more strands are added, we can gain confidence. For example, we might have the presence of trace conditioning behaviour, avoidance of noxious stimuli, and the presence of appropriately complex neural processing units. Though each of these types of evidence alone may be poorly supported, when taken together they are stronger, and in this case we would infer the presence of consciousness as the best explanation of our results.

Even where we may never have complete confidence in the validity of our measures, we can still identify which we consider to be more or less valid, based on the degree to which they have been tested and how well independent measures correlate with one another.

This is in line with the "facilitation hypothesis" advocated by the philosopher Jonathan Birch. Here, we take an assumption that consciousness facilitates a cluster of cognitive abilities, and can thus look for the presence or absence of a number of abilities within this cluster to strengthen or weaken the case for the presence of consciousness in some entity under investigation.

For animals, there is a further resource. Anatomical, physiological, and evolutionary similarities provide justification for believing that there is also similarity in conscious experience. The claim that we could never empirically settle whether organisms such as fishes feel pain underestimates the empirical and theoretical toolkit of biological science.

Being able to identify the limitations of our methods, and the background assumptions needed to justify their use, allows us to then work to overcome them. In particular, the ability to identify tests with independent background assumptions and to use them together will strengthen our confidence in the results of consciousness science.

Our argument is not intended to impede research into the measurement of consciousness. Rather, we see it as a call to analyse and improve our methods accordingly, with the hope that one day we may be able to solve the measurement problem of consciousness.
